messages.author: 82e8106f84fe4fab
messages.subject: Number of gradient evaluation
parts:
Hi all,

I am trying to make a comparison between random-walk Metropolis (RWM) and NUTS (RStan) similar to what was conducted in section 4.5 of the following paper.

Hoffman, Matthew D., and Andrew Gelman. "The No-U-turn sampler: adaptively setting path lengths in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo." Journal of Machine Learning Research 15.1 (2014): 1593-1623.

In the paper, the comparison was made based on the number of gradient evaluation, i.e NUTS was ran with 1000 iterations which required about 1,000,000 gradient evaluation. RWM was then ran for 1,000,000 iterations. My question is how can I determine the number of gradient evaluation in RStan? Is it similar to the number of leapfrog updates? In other words, I could extract the number of gradient evaluation using the following

sp <- get_sampler_params(fit) # fit is the stanfit object after running stan
head(sp[[1]]) 
    accept_stat__ stepsize__ treedepth__ n_leapfrog__ divergent__ energy__
[1,]     1.0000000  0.1250000           2            7                               0 286.9408
[2,]     0.5000000 14.3855101           0            1                              1 224.2364
[3,]     0.5000000  7.9001586           0            1                               1 208.4543
[4,]     0.5000000  3.4442552           0            1                               1 209.0779

Does this mean that the number of gradient evaluation for the 1st chain would be the sum of all numbers under n_leapfrog (column 4 of sp[[1]])?

Thanks in advance

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Number of gradient evaluation
parts:
Yes.  n_leapfrog is the total number of gradient evaluations
attempted in each transition.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Number of gradient evaluation
parts:
I looked in the JMLR paper and Adrian's right --- 1M density/gradient
evals for 1000 warmup and 1000 sampling iterations. So that's
a tree depth of 9 or so.

I wonder how the latest version we have in Stan would compare.

I also wonder how many of those 1000 warmup iterations were
actually necessary, if you really want to compare speed.

- Bob
